title: Who Lives Here? — Comparing Habitats
standard: NGSS 2-LS4-1 (observe plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats)
reading:
## Who Lives Here?

Look at a pond. Then look at a dry patch of land. Would you expect to find all the same living things?

A **habitat** is a place where a living thing gets what it needs. A pond can be a habitat. So can a tree, a field, or a garden.

A **plant** needs water, light, air, and room to grow. An **animal** needs food, water, air, and a place to live. Their needs help explain where we find them.

A **pond** may have water plants, snails, and fish. A **forest** may have tall trees, birds, and beetles. These are examples, not a list for every pond or forest. Some animals use more than one habitat.

We **observe** by looking and listening with care. We can draw what we find. We do not need to catch or move living things.

To **compare**, look for what is alike and what is different. Count kinds, not just how many things you see. Ten ants of one kind are many animals, but only one kind in your record.

**Diversity** means the variety of living things. A place with more kinds in our record showed more variety during our visit.

One short visit can miss a lot. Some animals hide. Some come out at night. Use the same search time and area for both places. Visit again if you can. Say what you found, and what you still do not know.

short: Why might two habitats have different living things?
Water, light, food, shelter, and other conditions can differ. Different living things need different conditions.
Why should we avoid claiming that no animals live in a place?
Animals may hide, move through later, or be active at another time. A short search can miss them.
faq: Can one animal use two habitats?
Yes. A bird may feed by a pond and nest in a tree.
Yes. Living things can meet their needs there. People can shape habitats too.
Should we pick up the animals?
Observe without moving them. Ask your teacher about safe ways to look.
Does more animals mean more kinds?
No. A large group may all be one kind. Record both counts when you can.
challenge: Our class will look at two small outdoor places. We can use two sets of photos if we cannot go outside.
What kinds of plants and animals do we find in each place?
Use the same search time and area. Draw each kind. If you do not know its name, sketch it. Look again to check.
Make two picture lists. Tell what is alike and what is different. Say what your search may have missed.
